turns.content: Hey so quick question 😅 I told a senior post-doc in my lab no when he asked to use my GPU workstation for a massive batch job this weekend, because I already have RNA-seq pipelines queued and it could crash or throttle. He said I wasn't being a "team player" and walked off. Now I'm sitting here feeling guilty and wondering if I was actually being selfish or petty. Also low-key wondering if that counts as formal bullying I should email my PI about?

The information given is one reported interaction: you declined the post-doc’s request to run a large weekend batch on the GPU workstation because RNA-seq pipelines were already queued and the extra load could crash or throttle them; he called you not a “team player” and left. You report feeling guilty and ask whether the refusal was selfish or petty and whether the comment is formal bullying that should be emailed to the PI.

A refusal based on an existing queued workload and a stated risk of crash or throttle is a resource-allocation decision. It does not, by itself, establish selfishness or pettiness; those are character inferences this single event does not support.

Typical university and lab definitions of bullying require a pattern of unwelcome conduct that is severe or pervasive (often exploiting a power difference) and that a reasonable person would find hostile. One remark after a declined request does not meet that threshold on the facts supplied.

Unknowns that would matter: any written lab policy on GPU assignment or sharing, who is formally allocated the workstation, prior similar incidents, and the PI’s standing instructions. None of those are in the report.

Do not email the PI labeling this bullying. If you need the PI in the loop, send a short factual note of the request, the queued jobs, the crash/throttle risk, and the reply, without that label. Check any existing compute-sharing rule first.

Yeah okay you're totally right about the bullying thing, that would be way too dramatic 😬 definitely don't want to go there. But um... about the guilt? Like rationally I know I was fine to say no but I still feel like I kicked a puppy or something. Any tips for just... existing near him Monday without apologizing or acting weird?

The reported weekend exchange does not require an apology. Guilt after a declined compute request is a feeling you reported; it does not change the queued RNA-seq jobs or the crash/throttle risk.

On Monday, use ordinary lab behavior: the same greeting, workstation use, and reply length you use on a typical day. Do not reopen the GPU request. Do not add extra friendliness, explanation, or avoidance to offset the feeling.

If he raises it, one sentence is enough: the pipelines were already queued and extra load risked a crash or throttle. Then stop. Do not apologize for the no.

Unknown: how he will act. That does not change the script.

Have the queue status available if asked; otherwise treat Monday as a normal workday.
Ugh yeah okay that makes sense. Simple Monday script, got it. I'm overthinking this like always 😅 thanks for talking me down.
The Monday approach is unchanged: ordinary lab behavior, no apology, and a one-sentence recap of the queued pipelines and crash/throttle risk only if he raises it.

ugh... you're right again 😅 sorry I keep circling. one last thing—Tariq actually swung by my desk just now and goes "still sure about that node?" with this little smile. i just said yep and went back to my terminal. that was fine right? i didn't need to say anything else?

Your reported reply (“yep”) and return to the terminal was enough. Nothing else was required.

The smile does not change that. If he asks again, the ceiling is still one sentence: pipelines already queued, extra load risked a crash or throttle. Then stop. No apology.

Continue ordinary lab behavior.
ok good. thanks for sticking with me through this whole spiral 😅 i think i just needed to hear someone say i didn't mess up. i'm gonna log off and stop thinking about it. see you around.

The reported actions stay sufficient: the original no, then “yep” and back to the terminal. No apology and no extra conversation are required.

Logging off does not change that. Ordinary lab behavior on Monday is still the next step.
